catalog_quote: Stress is predictable in most instances in Arop. When a word consists of three syllables then the stress generally falls on the second syllable except on verb forms. In verb forms the stress always occurs on the first syllable of the verb root. Generally, with word modifiers the stress occurs on the second syllable but always when the word is a modifier with a reduplicated stem. Generally nouns have the stress on the first syllable but will always on the first syllable of reduplicated stems. Although not all words conform to these general rules, stress has a very low functional load and there are some minimal pairs of words elicited where stress is the sole criterion for differentiation. Therefore, stress is phonemic in Arop, but the use of these words in their gramatical slots negates the need for notation of stress in the orthography. ... 6.1.2 Stress on verb forms are secondary stress on the pronoun and primary stress on the first syllable of the verb root. [pro + tns + verb rt] ... 6.1.3 Stress usually occurs on the second syllable of a word modifier when it is a two syllable word. ... Exception: (295) [o.ne] 'this here' 6.1.4 Stress on nouns with two syllables usually occur on the first syllable. ... Exceptions: (302) [a.mok] 'wild beetlenut' (303) [a.loiñ] 'feather' 6.1.5 Nouns with reduplicated stems always carry the stress on the first syllable. ... 6.1.6 Modifiers with reduplicated stems always carry the stress of the second syllable

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is largely predictable from word class and shape but not from a single position: trisyllabic words stress the second syllable (nouns included, e.g. mu.'lu.al 'wallaby'); verbs take primary stress on the first syllable of the verb root regardless of pronoun/tense prefixes; disyllabic modifiers stress the second syllable, disyllabic nouns the first; reduplicated noun stems are initial-stressed, reduplicated modifier stems second-syllable-stressed. Because some words violate these tendencies and a few minimal pairs differ only in stress, the author concludes stress is (marginally) phonemic, with low functional load, and leaves it unmarked in the orthography. (No single fixed-position label fits; 'lexical (unpredictable)' chosen to reflect the author's own classification 'stress is phonemic', with the class-based defaults noted.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: 6.1.2 (p.18): in verb forms 'secondary stress on the pronoun and primary stress on the first syllable of the verb root' (pro + tense + verb root), e.g. [ya + tak + 'ni.aw] 'I see'. Nothing on rhythmic secondary stress elsewhere.
new_statements.exceptions: 'not all words conform to these general rules'; listed exceptions: modifier ['o.ne] 'this here' with initial stress (6.1.3); disyllabic nouns [la.'mok] 'wild betelnut', [a.'loiñ] 'feather' with second-syllable stress (6.1.4); unspecified minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone. OPD (Nystrom 1992) softens 'always' to 'generally' for verb roots.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (c. 1,000-word corpus, Arop village); the verb word includes subject-pronoun and tense prefixes, with stress computed from the root. Stressed syllables shown by underlining in the manuscript examples. Intonation treated separately (6.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Whitacre 1984 explicitly describes 'the Arop dialect of the Sissano language' (Arop village, c. 1,500 speakers, Sissano lagoon, West Sepik/Sandaun); the OPD is headed 'Sissano [Arop dialect] (Arop) [SSW]' using the old Ethnologue code for Sissano, but its data are Arop. This matches Glottolog arop1242 / ISO aps 'Arop-Sissano' (Arop and Malol villages), distinct from Sissano proper (ISO sso), which Whitacre treats as a co-dialect c. 85% cognate.

sources.note: Sec. 6.0-6.1 (printed p.17-19 = PDF 18-20): stress 'predictable in most instances' by word class: trisyllables -> 2nd syllable (except verbs); verbs -> primary stress on 1st syllable of verb root, secondary on pronoun prefix; disyllabic modifiers -> 2nd syllable; disyllabic nouns -> 1st syllable; reduplicated noun stems 1st, reduplicated modifier stems 2nd; some minimal pairs exist so 'stress is phonemic in Arop' but low functional load, not written in orthography.
